name: Pomegranate extract

lead: Pomegranate extract concentrates the fruit's polyphenols, mainly ellagitannins, and is sold as a supplement and as an antioxidant in skincare. People use it for a clearer, more even, healthier-looking complexion.

Ellagitannins are converted by gut bacteria into urolithins, which are studied for anti-inflammatory activity, and polyphenols scavenge free radicals in lab assays. Most research is in cells, rodents and metabolic studies in people. A trial on skin aging and inflammation is registered, with no published result in the sources reviewed.

paras: Taken as a capsule or juice-based supplement or applied in serums and creams as a daily antioxidant, with changes judged over weeks to months.

No specific safety concerns with oral extract were found in the sources reviewed. The FDA and FTC have acted against unsupported disease claims by a major juice marketer. Responses differ between people because gut microbiota differ.

angle.text: Pomegranate extract delivers ellagitannin antioxidants, taken orally or applied, so oxidative skin stress falls and skin looks brighter and healthier. Its chemistry is well studied in the lab, and a skin-aging trial is registered.

lead: Pomegranate extract is a concentrate of polyphenols obtained from the fruit, peel or seeds of Punica granatum, a tree native to the region spanning the Caucasus and the Iranian plateau [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement and used in skincare as an antioxidant, with marketing built on its ellagitannin content.

The most abundant phytochemicals in the juice are ellagitannins, also called punicalagins, together with anthocyanins such as delphinidin and cyanidin [1]. After ingestion, gut bacteria convert ellagitannins to urolithins, and people differ in which urolithin "metabotype" they produce [2][3].

Laboratory studies show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity [4][5]. Wikipedia notes that research data are limited and that the US FDA and FTC have taken action over unproven health claims made by one major pomegranate juice marketer [1]. A registered trial on skin aging and inflammation exists, but its results are not summarized in the sources reviewed [6].

paras: Pomegranate was domesticated roughly 5,000 years ago in ancient Iran and has a long place in cuisine and religious symbolism across Persian, Egyptian and Mediterranean cultures [1]. Beyond the juice, the peel is rich in polyphenols, condensed tannins and catechins, which makes it a source for supplement extracts, while the seed oil is high in punicic acid [1].

Pomegranate extract is promoted for antioxidant support, sun-related skin aging and a brighter complexion, both as a pill and in serums and creams. The evidence behind these claims in the sources reviewed is mostly laboratory and metabolic research; direct appearance outcomes in people have not been reported there.

A pomegranate extract and its metabolite urolithin A reduced inflammation in a rat colitis model [2]. A separate rat study found that an ellagic acid-enriched extract attenuated chronic colonic inflammation [7]. Anthocyanidins from the fruit showed free-radical scavenging in a chemical assay [4]. In healthy volunteers, a standardized extract was studied for absorption, metabolism and antioxidant effects of its polyphenols [5]. Individual variation in gut microbiota metabolism of ellagitannins into urolithin metabotypes has been linked with differences in cardiometabolic biomarker responses [3][8]. Pomegranate ellagitannin-derived metabolites were reported to inhibit prostate cancer cell growth and localize to mouse prostate tissue [9].

In February 2010 the FDA sent a warning letter to POM Wonderful for making unproven claims about disease effects, and in 2016 the Federal Trade Commission ruled that the company could not make certain health claims in advertising; these actions concerned marketing claims, not safety [1].

Human work in the sources reviewed centers on pharmacokinetics and cardiometabolic markers. A randomized clinical trial grouped overweight and obese participants by urolithin metabotype to explain variability in cardiovascular risk biomarker responses to pomegranate [3]. A study in healthy volunteers examined absorption and antioxidant effects of an extract [5]. Registered trials include a phase 1 pharmacokinetic study in 20 healthy subjects [10], a trial in colorectal cancer patients [11], and a completed trial of 75 participants on pomegranate effects on skin aging and inflammation, listed with conditions of skin photoaging and inflammation [6]. The skin trial results are not available in the sources reviewed, so no conclusion about skin appearance can be stated.
